To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the domestic cat is the only model system for which loudness and recruitment have been characterized behaviorally, and that this species exhibits features of loudness coding that are similar to those that have previously been reported for humans.

the cats' reaction time measures of loudness perception reproduced well-known features, and the cats' reaction to loud sound exposure was similar to the effects of hearing loss in humans, and the cats showed the effects of speech structure and hearing aid amplification on loudness recruitment

(a) loudness perception in the domestic cat resembles that in humans, (b) exposure to intense sound produces loudness recruitment effects similar to those in humans, and (c) vowel sounds produce greater recruitment than pure tones, and the effects are exacerbated by the selective enhancement of speech structure.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the domestic cat is an adequate physiological model of loud noise-induced hearing loss and the behavioral correlates of hearing loss.
the cat is an excellent model for studying the physiological mechanisms underlying the perception of loudness.
the cat is a useful animal model for human hearing and hearing disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel behavioral task for assessing loudness in cats, and we have used that technique to characterize loudness and loudness recruitment in the cat.
the cat is a good model for loudness perception in humans, but that the model is not as good for recruitment effects.
cats have similar loudness perception to that in humans, but the loudness of vowels is more affected by hearing loss than tones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cats are a useful model for understanding loudness perception in humans.
cats have a very similar perception of loudness to humans, which is not surprising as we share many of the same auditory structures.
loudness perception is a complex function of sound intensity and frequency that is not fully captured by the simple power function used in most clinical audiometers.
